newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: MINISTER PREDICTS MORE WILL TAKE OUT HEALTH INSURANCE
Federal Health Minister Michael Wooldridge says he expects up to two percent of the population to take out health insurance this week, to avoid paying the higher Medicare levy.
People earning more than $50,000 a year will have to pay an extra one percent of their income to Medicare, unless they have private health insurance.
Doctor Wooldridge says it makes good sense economically and in terms of health, to take out private health cover.
He says people on higher incomes either give the money to the Tax Office or do something for themselves and their families and get private health cover.
The Minister says he thinks the majority of them will take out cover.
TAX OFFICE CRACKDOWN ON INVESTMENT PROPERTIES
The Tax Office is cracking down on claims relating to investment properties in an effort to claw back tens of millions of dollars in wrongly claimed tax deductions.
It's sending out warning letters to 100,000 real-estate investors this week, and is also contacting 5,000 tax agents who specialise in this area.
The move follows a Tax Office audit which found 60 per cent of people made wrong claims relating to investment properties.
Assistant Tax Commissioner, Allan Histon, says the education program will be followed up with an audit of about 6,000 people in the next year.
He says the main problem is owners of investment properties claiming capital improvements as repairs, which is not tax deductible.
Mr Histon says owners of investment properties can't claim things like putting up a new fence, as repairs.
Another problem he says is property investors charging non-commercial rates of rent to relatives and friends.
LIBERALS HAVE RESERVATIONS ABOUT GST REFERENDUM
Federal Liberal MP Wilson Tuckey says a national plebiscite on a Goods and Services Tax couldn't just be dumped on people.
The option was raised during last week's party-room talks on tax reform and Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith says it has some support within the Government.
Mr Tuckey says a GST, along with all other aspects of tax reform, should be given maximum exposure, to build public confidence.
He says his preference is for a parliamentary inquiry where people can give their evidence and express their concerns, but he wouldn't object to a plebiscite after that.
GOVT HAPPY TO FIGHT ELECTION ON WORK FOR DOLE SCHEME
Federal Schools Minister David Kemp says the Government would be happy to fight an election on its Work for the Dole Scheme.

The Government says it will return its Work for the Dole bill to the Senate in three months, thereby setting a trigger for a double dissolution election, to reverse amendments forced by Labor and the Democrats.
The Opposition parties successfully amended the bill in the Senate on Friday, and will be seeking further amendments today.
Doctor Kemp has told ABC Radio the Government doesn't want an election, but will fight one on the Work for the Dole scheme if it has to.
He says it's good legislation, based on a principle of mutual obligation between unemployed people and the community.
Doctor Kemp says many people in the community are working hard to provide support for unemployed people, and it's fair that they should be asked to put something back into the community.
QLY MAY RESTRICT ABORTIONS TO HOSPITALS
Queensland Health Minister, Mike Horan, says the State Government is likely to restrict abortions to hospitals only if it means more late-term abortions can be stopped.
The proposal to allow abortions to be performed only in hospitals has attracted strong criticism from some doctors.
They fear the proposal, contained in a report by Attorneys General, is a move to outlaw abortion services.
But Mr Horan has defended the idea.
He says the Government will look closely at the report, if the proposal means that late term abortions that have occurred in some clinics, will be stopped.
Mr Horan says at some clinics, babies over 20 weeks of age have been killed by the cranial decompression method and then aborted, and that is a terrible practice.
BANK WINS APPROVAL FOR RETIREMENT ACCOUNTS
The Colonial State Bank has become the first bank to receive official approval to establish Retirement Savings Accounts.

The Federal Government has legislated to allow banks, building societies, credit unions and life offices to offer retirement savings accounts from July the first, to inject more competition in the superannuation industry.
Colonial's Stuart James says RSAs will provide a low cost, low risk, "bank pass-book" style of saving for retirement.
Other financial institutions are also expected to soon gain approval to provide this service.
ECONOMISTS' PUSH FOR REDUCED GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSIONS
The Australia Institite has released a statement signed by 131 economists that Australia can reduce greenhouse gas emissions, without harming the economy.

While the Federal Government argues for a more lenient greenhouse gas reduction targets for Australia, the statement says it is equitable and efficient for countries with higher per capita emissions to reduce their emissions by more.
The statement coincides with the start of the Earth Summit in New York, where climate change policies will be debated.
US President Bill Clinton and British Prime Minister Tony Blair will be among the world leaders attending the Summit.
Australia will be represented by Environment Minister Robert Hill.
